back: Treating employees as a resource to be used efficiently, with tight control, targets and flexible numbers to keep labour cost low.
Treating employees as assets whose commitment is developed through communication, training, participation and reward.
No guaranteed hours; the worker is paid only for hours worked. Maximum flexibility for the employer; insecurity for the worker.
A total number of hours over the year, scheduled to match demand; fewer overtime payments but harder to plan.
Part-time, temporary, flexi-time, compressed hours, job sharing, home working, shift working and the gig economy.
They lower cost and match labour to demand but can reduce commitment, security and loyalty and raise turnover.
Recruitment screening, monitoring, e-learning and workforce planning: faster and cheaper, but risks of bias, privacy loss and mistrust.
Hard suits routine work and tight margins; soft suits skilled work where service and ideas matter. Most firms use a mix.

front: Hours and cost for flexible labour
back: Hours needed = weeks × hours per week for each period, added; cost = hours × rate (rate × (1 + premium) for zero-hours).
